On Aug 21, 2012, at 12:57 PM, Cory Atwood wrote:

The upper and lower limits of for statements must be data. It is not allowed for them to be expressions that turn out to be of fixed value.  I am not sure where in the manual this is stated.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] interesting bit from the bugs newsgroup
parts:
On 8/26/12 7:10 AM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>
> On Aug 21, 2012, at 12:57 PM, Cory Atwood wrote:
>>
>> The upper and lower limits of for statements must be data. It is not allowed for them to be expressions that turn out
>> to be of fixed value. I am not sure where in the manual this is stated.

I knew they had to be data. That's just so BUGS
can figure out the structure of the graphical model
as the data's read in.

Can't the bounds be expressions of data, too?

We only require the dimensions of arrays, vectors
and matrices to be expressions of data.

Christian Robert pointed out on his blog that the
R program:

for (n in 1:10) {
n <- n + 1;
print(n);
}

prints the 10 numbers, 2, 3, ..., 11. The
modification n is active locally but isn't realted
to the loop variable. That's because they look
at loop variables as ranging over an array of values,
not as being incremented and tested like C++ or Fortran
for loops.

- Bob

On 8/26/12 8:29 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Yes, my point was that we can state this as an advantage of Stan (compared to Bugs) in the Stan-for-Bugs-Users chapter of the manual.

I just looked this up. WinBUGs allows expressions
in loops bound, as shown here:


for (j in culm[i - 1] + 1 : culm[i]) {

(from WinBUGS examples, Vol 1, LSAT model)

What they don't allow is parameters in the
expressions for the bounds.

We don't directly allow parameters there because
we don't have any integer parameters (yet, anyway).
We could have an integer derived from a real
parameter.

What's perhaps more to the point is that we can
redefine variables, so we don't need to declare
a gazillion nodes indexed by the loop they're
defined in. I think BUGS is just expanding the
graphical model out fully.

- Bob

FYI, JAGS extends BUGS in that it allows functions of data, e.g.,

for (j in max(J)) { ... }

where J is a vector passed in as data.
